description: We are an enthusiastic team of Computer Science students participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, driven by a passion for space exploration, artificial intelligence, Earth observation, and technological innovation. With experience in software development, cybersecurity, and AI, we aim to tackle real-world challenges using NASA's open data. We value creativity, teamwork, scientific accuracy, and impactful solutions, and welcome collaborators with diverse technical and research skills.
summary: FireChronicle is a web platform that turns NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections into a historical burning activity calendar for a South Sumatra-region pilot area (2019–2024, compared with 2025–2026). MODIS and VIIRS see fire differently: VIIRS recorded 148,913 quality-filtered detections where MODIS recorded 31,781 over the same six years, so combining their counts would distort the fire history. FireChronicle processes both sensors on a common 0.25° grid and monthly timeline, maps detections per cell, and compares each month with its seasonal baseline to find unusually active periods. We then tested harmonization directly by predicting MODIS from VIIRS on held-out years. A monthly ratio beat ignoring VIIRS in 6 of 6 years, but beat a single ratio in only 3 of 6, so we keep the sensors separate rather than publish an unreliable merged series. Finally, every "unusual month" is re-tested across five analysis configurations: 6 of 72 months stay elevated in all of them, while 26 change with the method. FireChronicle shows not just when fire activity was high, but which conclusions you can trust.
details:
Here's the full Project Details text with ChatGPT included, ready to paste. Set the short headings in bold in the editor.

FireChronicle: Sensor - Aware Historical Fire Activity and Reliability Intelligence from NASA MODIS and VIIRS Team ZeroDay_Squad · NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots Live application: https://firechronicle-eight.vercel.app · Source code: https://github.com/alfaxgen10/FireChronicle

1. Background and problem MODIS and VIIRS are the two main sources of NASA active-fire detections, but they observe fire differently. VIIRS has 375 m pixels against about 1 km for MODIS, and the instruments differ in detection sensitivity and overpass times. In our South Sumatra-region pilot area, VIIRS recorded 148,913 quality-filtered detections in 2019–2024, while MODIS recorded 31,781 over the same months, 4.7 times fewer. The MODIS record also changes over time: it moves from Collection 6 (2019–2022) to Collection 6.1 (from 2023), and its median daytime detection times drift (Terra from about 10:35 to 08:39 local time, Aqua from about 13:41 to 15:43). Combining or switching between these records without accounting for these differences can produce false trends. A month can look unusual because of the sensor rather than the fire activity.

2. Objective and research questions Our objective was a historical burning activity calendar that keeps sensor differences visible and reports how far each conclusion can be trusted.

  • RQ1: Can MODIS and VIIRS be brought into a comparable regional series while keeping their provenance?
  • RQ2: How sensitive is the identification of unusually active months to the choice of sensor, grid resolution and threshold?
  • RQ3: Can an interactive map, calendar and reliability view make this evidence easy to inspect?

3. Data NASA FIRMS archive and near-real-time (NRT) active-fire detections for MODIS (Terra/Aqua, Collection 6/6.1) and VIIRS (NOAA-20, Collection 2). The period is January 2019 to October 2026; NRT files cover only VIIRS August–October 2026 and MODIS September–October 2026. The study area is a rectangular pilot box, 101.5°–106.0° E and 1.0°–4.9° S. Each source file is recorded in a manifest with its SHA-256 hash, row counts, product versions and coverage dates, and processing stops if a file does not match.

4. Methods

  1. Quality control. We validate schema, coordinates and timestamps, then remove low-confidence detections (MODIS confidence below 30; VIIRS "low") and duplicates.
    • MODIS primary (0.25°, 75th percentile);
    • MODIS coarse grid (0.5°);
    • MODIS strict threshold (90th percentile);
    • VIIRS 0.25°;
    • VIIRS 0.5°.

5. Results

  • Sensor comparison: the mean occupied-cell fraction is 19.5% for MODIS and 42.6% for VIIRS across the 72 overlapping months. Both sensors show the same seasonal cycle, with the fire season peaking in August–October and the strongest seasons in 2019 and 2023.
  • Harmonization (RQ1): mean absolute error of the predicted MODIS index was 6.6 percentage points with the monthly ratio, 7.3 with a single ratio and 9.7 without VIIRS. The monthly ratio beat the no-VIIRS baseline in 6 of 6 held-out years, but beat the single ratio in only 3 of 6. VIIRS carries real information about MODIS activity, but the relationship is not stable enough over six years to justify a merged series. VIIRS also levels off near 80% of cells occupied in peak months, which limits any simple ratio. We therefore keep MODIS and VIIRS as separate records and do not publish a harmonized series. This result evaluates a predictive relationship only; it does not establish sensor equivalence, calibration or validated fusion.
  • Reliability (RQ2): of the 72 months in 2019–2024, 6 are consistently elevated, 26 are classification-sensitive and 40 are not elevated. More than a third of months, concentrated in the fire season, change classification with the analysis choice. A leave-one-year-out check with the 90th-percentile configuration changed 3 of 72 classifications and no reported stability label.
  • Recent activity: against the frozen 2019–2024 reference, MODIS shows 9 of 10 and VIIRS 7 of 10 elevated months in January–October 2026. Both sensors agree for January, March and June–October 2026, which is the strongest evidence that those months were genuinely more active. February and May are elevated only in MODIS and are flagged for caution, given the MODIS record changes described above.

6. Validation and reproducibility

  • Tests: 372 automated tests (335 Python, 37 frontend) cover ingestion, confidence filtering, grid geometry, missing-data handling, baselines, every combination of the reliability rule, the data contracts and the user interface.
  • Map data check: the per-cell map data are built from the raw FIRMS files and must reproduce the released monthly detection counts and occupied cells exactly. They do, for all 94 months of both sensors.
  • Clean rebuild: the release was rebuilt and tested from a clean copy.
  • Open outputs: all outputs are versioned JSON files with provenance, available as CSV/JSON downloads.

7. Application The web application connects the analysis into one path:

  • Overview: a regional detection map with sensor, year and month filters.
  • Explore: detections per cell for any month, with that month's baseline and anomaly.
  • Historical calendar: a year × month heatmap per sensor, with month details and trends.
  • Reliability lab: the MODIS–VIIRS comparison, harmonization results and stability labels.
  • Methodology & export: data sources, processing steps, limitations and downloads.

8. Creativity Sensor calibration, anomaly detection and uncertainty assessment each have prior work, and we make no claim to be first. Our contribution is to combine them in one transparent, user-facing tool. Instead of giving a single answer to "which months were unusual?", FireChronicle tests harmonization on held-out data and reports when a result depends on the sensor or method. This distinguishes findings that hold across sensors and methods from those that don't.

9. Impact

  • Fire and haze researchers: can see season timing and unusual years with sensor effects separated.
  • Regional land managers: can see which periods recur and how much confidence each finding deserves.
  • Educators: have a worked example of using satellite records carefully.
  • Limits of use: the tool supports retrospective understanding. It is not a fire-detection, alert or forecasting system, and its adoption has not been tested.

10. Limitations and factors considered

  • Hotspots are satellite detections, not individual fires, burned area or severity.
  • The occupied-cell fraction is an unweighted grid index, not an area measure.
  • The baseline covers six years, and classifications are in-sample.
  • The study area is a rectangular box, not verified against provincial boundaries, with no land/water mask.
  • The FIRMS type field is not filtered, so static, offshore and volcano sources are included. These are 3.1% of VIIRS detections, changing any month's index by at most 2.8 percentage points.
  • NRT months are less comparable with the archive-based reference.

All of these are disclosed in the application.

11. Tools and technologies

  • Analysis: Python with pandas, NumPy, SciPy and pytest.
  • Web: TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet and Apache ECharts; data validated with Zod.
  • Hosting: code on GitHub, site on Vercel.
  • Data: NASA FIRMS; map tiles from OpenStreetMap.
  • AI assistance: Kiro and GitHub Copilot were used as coding assistants. ChatGPT was used for project planning documents, proposal text and interface design suggestions. Kiro also helped prepare the presentation slides. All scientific results are computed from NASA data by the project code, as described in the repository README.
  • Hardware: none.

12. Future work

  • A longer MODIS baseline from 2001, with the collection change handled explicitly.
  • A detection-level layer with confidence and day/night filters.
  • Additional regions with verified boundaries.
  • An evidence-grounded AI assistant that answers only from verified results.
